1.o: The history of Samuel here begins as early as that of Samson did, even before he was born, as afterwards the history of John the Baptist and our blessed Saviour. Some of the scripture-worthies drop out of the clouds, as it were, and their first appearance is in their full growth and lustre. But others are accounted for from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception. What God says of the prophet Jeremiah is true of all: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee," Jer. i. 5.
1.i: Hannah prayed silently at Shiloh for a child, was misunderstood by the priest, then blessed by him, and gave birth to Samuel.
1.p: Lord, You hear prayers that have no words. Hear us today, and help us to leave our burdens with You. Amen.
1.l: Tell God honestly about something that is making you sad. He hears prayers that have no sound.
q: Elkanah went yearly though he did not have to. What do you do every year that no one requires?

2.o: In this chapter we have, I. Hannah's song of thanksgiving to God for his favour to her in giving her Samuel, ver. 1-10. II. Their return to their family, with Eli's blessing, ver. 11, 20. The increase of their family, ver. 21. Samuel's growth and improvement (ver. 11, 18, 21, 26), and the care Hannah took to clothe him, ver. 19. III. The great wickedness of Eli's sons, ver. 12-17, 22. IV. The over-mild reproof that Eli gave them for it, ver. 23-25. V.
2.i: First Samuel 1 and 2 follow Hannah to Shiloh to keep a promise, and show how she answered God's gift with a song.
2.p: Lord, every good gift comes from You. Teach us to give back what You have given, and to rejoice in You. Amen.
2.l: Give something you love to someone else today, and thank God for it.
q: What good thing in your life do you need to hold with open hands?

3.o: In the foregoing chapter we had Samuel a young priest, though by birth a Levite only, for he ministered before the Lord in a linen ephod; in this chapter we have him a young prophet, which was more, God in an extraordinary manner revealing himself to him, and in him reviving, if not commencing, prophecy in Israel. Here is, I. God's first manifestation of himself in an extraordinary manner to Samuel, ver. 1-10. II. The message he sent by him to Eli, ver. 11-14. III.
3.i: First Samuel 3 describes the night a boy first heard God's voice, in a time when hearing it had become rare.
3.p: Speak, Lord, Your servant is listening. Help us to hear You, and to say what You give us to say, even when it is hard. Amen.
3.l: Take a quiet minute today, and say to God, Speak, I am listening.
q: Samuel served as a child according to his place and capacity. What can you do well now, where you are?

4.o: The predictions in the foregoing chapters concerning the ruin of Eli's house here begin to be fulfilled; how long after does not appear, but certainly not long. Such sinners God often makes quick work with. Here is, I. The disgrace and loss Israel sustained in an encounter with the Philistines, ver. 1, 2. II. Their foolish project to fortify themselves by bringing the ark of God into their camp upon the shoulders of Hophni and Phinehas (ver. 3, 4), which made them secure (ver.
4.i: Israel carried the ark into battle as a lucky charm, lost the battle and the ark, and learned that the ark could not do what only God could do.
4.p: Lord, You are not a charm in our pocket. Teach us to trust You, not the things that remind us of You. Amen.
4.l: Be careful about using good things like a lucky charm. Today, talk to God instead of just holding onto something special.
q: They might have asked the prophet and did not. Whose counsel are you passing over because of their age or position?

5.o: It is now time to enquire what has become of the ark of God; we cannot but think that we shall hear more of that sacred treasure. I should have thought the next news would have been that all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, had gathered together as one man, with a resolution to bring it back, or die in the attempt; but we find not any motion made of that kind, so little was there of zeal or courage left among them.
5.s: The Ark Goes Home on a Cart
5.i: The Philistines send the captured ark home on a cart pulled by two cows, and it comes to Beth-shemesh.
5.p: Lord, You are greater than any idol. Bring us home when we are far away. Amen.
5.l: Thank God today for something He brought back to you after you thought it was lost.
q: The Philistines' own priests told them to send the ark back. What does that tell you about who God is?

6.o: In this chapter we have the return of the ark to the land of Israel, whither we are now gladly to attend it, and observe, I. How the Philistines dismissed it, by the advice of their priests (ver. 1-11), with rich presents to the God of Israel, to make an atonement for their sin (ver. 3-5), and yet with a project to bring it back, unless Providence directed the kine, contrary to their inclination, to go to the land of Israel, ver. 8, 9. II. How the Israelites entertained it. 1.
6.s: The Ark Goes Home on a Cart
6.i: The Philistines send the captured ark home on a cart pulled by two cows, and it comes to Beth-shemesh.
6.p: Lord, You are greater than any idol. Bring us home when we are far away. Amen.
6.l: Thank God today for something He brought back to you after you thought it was lost.
q: The Philistines' own priests told them to send the ark back. What does that tell you about who God is?

7.o: In this chapter we have, I. The eclipsing of the glory of the ark, by its privacy in Kirjath-jearim for many years, ver. 1, 2. II. The appearing of the glory of Samuel in his public services for the good of Israel, to whom he was raised up to be a judge, and he was the last that bore that character. This chapter gives us all the account we have of him when he was in the prime of his time; for what we had before was in his childhood (ch. ii. and iii.); what we have of him after was in his old age, ch. viii. 1.
7.s: Thus Far the Lord Has Helped Us
7.i: After twenty years of mourning, Israel returned to the Lord at Mizpah, God thundered the Philistines into panic, and Samuel set up a stone called Ebenezer.
7.p: Lord, thus far You have helped us. Thank You for the places we remember, and keep us trusting You for what lies ahead. Amen.
7.l: Find a small stone, a shell, or a card, and write on it: Thus far the Lord has helped me. Keep it where you can see it.
q: Ebenezer marks a place of help at the site of an old defeat. Where has God helped you?

8.o: Things went so very well with Israel, in the chapter before, under Samuel's administration, that, methinks, it is a pity to find him so quickly, as we do in this chapter, old, and going off, and things working towards a revolution. But so it is; Israel's good days seldom continue long. We have here, I. Samuel decaying, ver. 1. II. His sons degenerating, ver. 2, 3. III. Israel discontented with the present government and anxious to see a change. For 1. They petition Samuel to set a king over them, ver. 4, 5. 2.
8.i: When Samuel grew old and his sons failed, Israel demanded a king like other nations, and God warned them what a king would cost.
8.p: Lord, You are our true King. Keep us from wanting what everyone else wants, and teach us to trust Your way. Amen.
8.l: Think about something you really want. Ask God if it is good for you, and tell Him you will accept His answer.
q: The people asked for a king to be like everyone else. Where do you want to be like everyone else instead of following God?

9.o: Samuel had promised Israel, from God, that they should have a king; it is strange that the next news is not of candidates setting up for the government, making an interest in the people, or recommending themselves to Samuel, and, by him, to God, to be put in nomination. Why does not the prince of the tribe of Judah, whoever he is, look about him now, remembering Jacob's entail of the sceptre on that tribe? Is there never a bold aspiring man in Israel, to say, "I will be king, if God will choose me?"
9.i: Searching for lost donkeys, Saul came to Samuel, who had been told by God that he would arrive, and was honored as Israel's coming king.
9.p: Lord, You guide us in small things. Help us to see Your hand in ordinary days. Amen.
9.l: If you have a small errand to do today, do it well. God can use ordinary jobs to lead somewhere big.
q: The text praises Saul's looks and says nothing of his character. What do you praise in people first, and is it the right thing?

10.o: We left Samuel and Saul walking together, probably some private way over the fields down from Ramah, perhaps in the paths of the vineyards, and Saul expecting to hear from Samuel the word of God. Now here we have, I. The anointing of Saul then and there, ver. 1. The signs Samuel gave him, ver. 2-6. And instructions, ver. 7-8. II. The accomplishment of those signs to the satisfaction of Saul, ver. 9-13. III. His return to his father's house, ver. 14-16. IV. His public election by lot, and solemn inauguration, ver.
10.i: Samuel anointed Saul with oil, gave him three signs that all came true that day, and Saul, changed by the Spirit, kept the news of his kingship quiet.
10.p: Lord, You call and equip. Give us humble hearts, and help us to keep what You begin in us. Amen.
10.l: Keep a secret that someone trusted you with, even a happy one, today.
q: Saul changed in a day but did not stay changed. How do you keep a good start going?

11.o: In this chapter we have the first-fruits of Saul's government, in the glorious rescue of Jabesh-Gilead out of the hands of the Ammonites. Let not Israel thence infer that therefore they did well to ask a king (God could and would have saved them without one); but let them admire God's goodness, that he did not reject them when they rejected him, and acknowledge his wisdom in the choice of the person whom, if he did not find fit, yet he made fit, for the great trust he called him to, and enabled, in some measure…
11.i: King Saul's first great act was rescuing the city of Jabesh-gilead, and its people never forgot it, even when they brought his body home years later.
11.p: Lord, thank You for those who have come to our rescue. Make us people who remember, and who rescue others. Amen.
11.l: Think of someone who helped you when you were in trouble. Thank them today, or draw them a thank-you note.
q: Jabesh remembered Saul for the rescue. Who has rescued you, and have you ever thanked them?

12.o: We left the general assembly of the states together, in the close of the foregoing chapter; in this chapter we have Samuel's speech to them, when he resigned the government into the hands of Saul, in which, I. He clears himself from all suspicion or imputation of mismanagement, while the administration was in his hands, ver. 1-5. II. He reminds them of the great things God had done for them and for their fathers, ver. 6-13. III. He sets before them good and evil, the blessing and the curse, ver. 14, 15. IV.
12.i: First Samuel 12 is a retirement speech that ends with thunder in the dry season.
12.p: Lord, You do not abandon Your people. Give us leaders with clean hands, and give us hearts that serve You fully. Amen.
12.l: Pray today for a leader you have trouble with, and ask God to help them.
q: Samuel could challenge anyone to name what he had taken. Could you say the same about your dealings with others?

13.o: Those that desired a king like all the nations fancied that, when they had one, they should look very great and considerable; but in this chapter we find it proved much otherwise. While Samuel was joined in commission with Saul things went well, ch. xi. 7. But, now that Saul began to reign alone, all went to decay, and Samuel's words began to be fulfilled: "You shall be consumed, both you and your king;" for never was the state of Israel further gone in a consumption than in this chapter. I.
13.i: First Samuel 13 shows the first crack in Saul's reign, caused by one afternoon of impatience.
13.p: Lord, teach us to wait for You. Give us patience when everything around us says to hurry. Amen.
13.l: Practice waiting today: when you want to rush something, stop for one full minute and ask God first.
q: The Philistines took away Israel's smiths so they could not make weapons. What skill or tool is someone keeping you from, and what are you doing about it?

14.o: We left the host of Israel in a very ill posture, in the close of the foregoing chapter; we saw in them no wisdom, nor strength, nor goodness, to give us ground to expect any other than that they should all be cut off by the army of the Philistines; yet here we find that infinite power which works without means, and that infinite goodness which gives without merit, glorified in a happy turn to their affairs, that still Samuel's words may be made good: "The Lord will not forsake his people, for his great name's…
14.i: Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed a cliff to attack a Philistine outpost, trusting that God can save by few as easily as by many, and God sent panic on the enemy.
14.p: Lord, give us courage like Jonathan's and the loyalty of his armor-bearer, and help us to trust You with small beginnings. Amen.
14.l: Be like the armor-bearer today. Tell a friend who is trying something brave: I'm with you.
q: Jonathan trusted that God can save with few as easily as with many. When do you think you need more before you can try?

15.o: In this chapter we have the final rejection of Saul from being king, for his disobedience to God's command in not utterly destroying the Amalekites. By his wars and victories he hoped to magnify and perpetuate his own name and honour, but, by his mismanagement of them, he ruined himself, and laid his honour in the dust. Here is, I. The commission God gave him to destroy the Amalekites, with a command to do it utterly, ver. 1-3. II. Saul's preparation for this expedition, ver. 4-6. III.
15.i: God told Saul to destroy Amalek completely, Saul spared the best and the king, and Samuel told him that obedience is better than sacrifice.
15.p: Lord, give us hearts that obey You, not just hearts that give You what we choose. Amen.
15.l: Follow one instruction today exactly as it was given, not close, but exactly, and notice how it feels.
q: Saul offered what he chose in place of what he was told. What are you offering God in place of obedience?

16.o: At this chapter begins the story of David, one that makes as great a figure in the sacred story as almost any of the worthies of the Old Testament, one that both with his sword and with his pen served the honour of God and the interests of Israel as much as most ever did, and was as illustrious a type of Christ. Here I. Samuel is appointed and commissioned to anoint a king among the sons of Jesse at Bethlehem, ver. 1-5. II. All his elder sons are passed by and David the youngest is pitched upon and anointed, ver.
16.s: The Lord Looks at the Heart
16.i: God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, and chooses David, the youngest son, who is out with the sheep.
16.p: Lord, You look at the heart. Make our hearts good, and help us to see people as You do. Amen.
16.l: Look for something good in the heart of someone today, and tell them what you see.
q: God picked the one nobody expected. Who might God be choosing that you have overlooked?

17.o: David is the man whom God now delights to honour, for he is a man after his own heart. We read in the foregoing chapter how, after he was anointed, Providence made him famous in the court; we read in this chapter how Providence made him much more famous in the camp, and, by both, not only marked him for a great man, but fitted him for the throne for which he was designed. In the court he was only Saul's physician; but in the camp Israel's champion; there he fairly fought, and beat Goliath of Gath.
17.s: A Giant in the Valley of Elah
17.i: A giant challenges Israel every morning and evening for forty days until young David arrives with bread for his brothers.
17.p: Lord, You are bigger than every giant. Help us to see You first. Amen.
17.l: When someone tries to scare you today, remember that God is bigger.
q: Everyone saw how big Goliath was. David saw how big God was. What do you see first?

18.o: In the course of the foregoing chapter we left David in triumph; now in this chapter we have, I. The improvement of his triumphs; he soon became, 1. Saul's constant attendant, ver. 2. 2. Jonathan's covenant friend, ver. 1, 3, 4. 3. The darling of his country, ver. 5, 7, 16. II. The allays of his triumphs. This is the vanity that accompanies even a right work, that "for it a man is envied," Eccl. iv. 4. So David was by Saul. 1. He hated him, and sought to kill him himself, ver. 8-11. 2.
18.i: First Samuel 18 and 20 follow the friendship of a king's son and a shepherd who would take his father's throne.
18.p: Lord, thank You for true friends. Help us to be faithful friends who keep our promises. Amen.
18.l: Keep a promise to a friend today, even if keeping it is not easy.
q: David looked on his love for Jonathan as a sacred thing. Which friendship do you treat as sacred and which as convenient?

19.o: Immediately after David's marriage, which one would have hoped would secure him Saul's affection, we find his troubles coming upon him faster than ever and Saul's enmity to him the cause of all. His death was vowed, and four fair escapes of his from the hurtful sword of Saul we have an account of in this chapter: the first by the prudent mediation of Jonathan (ver. 1-7), the second by his own quickness (ver. 8-10), the third by Michal's fidelity (ver.
19.s: Michal Lowers David from the Window
19.i: Saul tries to kill David, and Michal lowers David from a window and tricks the guards.
19.p: Lord, You protect Your servants in many ways. Make us brave and wise when we help the ones in danger. Amen.
19.l: Help a friend who is in trouble today, even if it takes some courage.
q: Michal helped David against her own father. What do you do when loyalties are divided?

20.o: David, having several times narrowly escaped Saul's fury, begins to consider at last whether it may not be necessary for him to retire into the country and to take up arms in his own defence. But he will not do so daring a thing without consulting his faithful friend Jonathan; how he did this, and what passed between them, we have an account in this chapter, where we have as surprising instances of supernatural love as we had in the chapter before of unnatural hatred. I.
20.i: First Samuel 18 and 20 follow the friendship of a king's son and a shepherd who would take his father's throne.
20.p: Lord, thank You for true friends. Help us to be faithful friends who keep our promises. Amen.
20.l: Keep a promise to a friend today, even if keeping it is not easy.
q: David looked on his love for Jonathan as a sacred thing. Which friendship do you treat as sacred and which as convenient?

21.o: David has now quite taken leave both of Saul's court and of his camp, has bidden farewell to his alter idem—his other self, the beloved Jonathan; and henceforward to the end of this book he is looked upon and treated as an outlaw and proclaimed a traitor. We still find him shifting from place to place for his own safety, and Saul pursuing him.
21.s: Bread and the Sword at Nob
21.i: First Samuel 21 finds David on the run, hungry and unarmed, asking a priest for help at the cost of a half-truth.
21.p: Lord, You see what we hide. Keep us honest, and give mercy to those who suffer for our mistakes. Amen.
21.l: Be completely honest today, even in a small thing, and see how it feels.
q: David asked for bread and a sword. What two things are you asking for that you also feel you can't take?

22.o: David, being driven from Achish, returns into the land of Israel to be hunted by Saul. I. David sets up his standard in the cave of Adullam, entertains his relations (ver. 1), enlists soldiers (ver. 2), but removes his aged parents to a more quiet settlement (ver. 3, 4), and has the prophet Gad for his counsellor, ver. 5. Saul resolves to pursue him and find him out, complains of his servants and Jonathan (ver.
22.i: David hides in the cave of Adullam, where his family and four hundred people in trouble gather around him.
22.p: Lord, You gather the distressed and make them strong. Use us to welcome people who are hurting. Amen.
22.l: Reach out to someone who seems to be in a hard place, and offer a kind word.
q: David led a band of people who had nowhere else to go. Who do you know who needs a place?

23.o: Saul, having made himself drunk with the blood of the priests of the Lord, is here, in this chapter, seeking David's life, who appears here doing good, and suffering ill, at the same time. Here is, I. The good service he did to his king and country, in rescuing the city of Keilah out of the hands of the Philistines, ver. 1-6. II. The danger he was thereby brought into from the malice of the prince he served and the treachery of the city he saved, and his deliverance, by divine direction, from that danger, ver.
23.i: David saves Keilah from the Philistines, asks the Lord about Saul's coming, and leaves before Saul can trap him.
23.p: Lord, we ask You for guidance. Show us what to do and where to go, and keep us from trusting the wrong people. Amen.
23.l: Before you decide something today, take a minute to ask God what to do.
q: David asked the Lord and got a clear answer. How do you ask God for guidance?

24.o: We have hitherto had Saul seeking an opportunity to destroy David, and, to his shame, he could never find it. In this chapter David had a fair opportunity to destroy Saul, and, to his honour, he did not make use of it; and his sparing Saul's life was as great an instance of God's grace in him as the preserving of his own life was of God's providence over him. Observe, I. How maliciously Saul sought David's life, ver. 1, 2. II.
24.s: A Corner of the Robe at En-gedi
24.i: David has the chance to harm Saul in a cave at En-gedi, cuts only his robe, and calls out to the king.
24.p: Lord, give us hearts like David's, that choose mercy when we have the power to hurt. Amen.
24.l: When you have a chance to get back at someone today, choose kindness and see what happens.
q: David had every excuse to harm Saul and refused. How do you respond when someone wrongs you?

25.o: We have here some intermission of David's troubles by Saul. Providence favoured him with a breathing time, and yet this chapter gives us instances of the troubles of David. If one vexation seems to be over, we must not be secure; a storm may arise from some other point, as here to David. I. Tidings of the death of Samuel could not but trouble him, ver. 1. But, II. The abuse he received from Nabal is more largely recorded in this chapter. 1. The character of Nabal, ver. 2, 3. 2. The humble request sent to him, ver.
25.i: Nabal insults David, and Abigail rides out with gifts and wise words to keep David from taking revenge.
25.p: Lord, You bless peacemakers. Make us wise and brave like Abigail. Amen.
25.l: Be a peacemaker today: when two people are arguing, help them calm down.
q: The request was a mixture of courtesy and defiance. When has a polite request actually been a demand?

26.o: David's troubles from Saul here begin again; and the clouds return after the rain, when one would have hoped the storm had blown over, and the sky had cleared upon that side; but after Saul had owned his fault in persecuting David, and acknowledged David's title to the crown, yet here he revives the persecution, so perfectly lost was he to all sense of honour and virtue. I. The Ziphites informed him where David was (ver. 1), and thereupon he marched out with a considerable force in quest of him, ver. 2, 3. II.
26.s: The Spear and the Water Jug
26.i: David takes Saul's spear and water jug in the night and spares him a second time, then calls out to show Saul what he did.
26.p: Lord, You are the judge of all. Keep us from taking revenge, and help us to leave things in Your hands. Amen.
26.l: When you have the chance to get back at someone, leave it to God, and be kind instead.
q: David did not need to take revenge to be safe. What does it look like to trust God with a hurt?

27.o: David was a man after God's own heart, and yet he had his faults, which are recorded, not for our imitation, but for our admonition; witness the story of this chapter, in which, though, I. We find, to his praise, that he prudently took care of his own safety and his family's (ver. 2-4) and valiantly fought Israel's battles against the Canaanites (ver. 8-9), yet, II. We find, to his dishonour, 1. That he began to despair of his deliverance, ver. 1. 2.
27.i: First Samuel 27 finds David on the run so long that he takes shelter with the people Israel had been fighting.
27.p: Lord, You protect Your people even when they take the wrong road. Keep us honest, and bring us safely home. Amen.
27.l: Tell the truth today in a situation where hiding something would be easier, and see how it feels.
q: David trusted a Philistine's promise when he could not trust Saul's. Whose word are you leaning on when someone closer has let you down?

28.o: Preparations are herein making for that war which will put an end to the life and reign of Saul, and so make way for David to the throne. In this war, I. The Philistines are the aggressors and Achish their king makes David his confidant, ver. 1, 2. II. The Israelites prepare to receive them, and Saul their king makes the devil his privy-counsellor, and thereby fills the measure of his iniquity. Observe, 1. The despairing condition which Saul was in, ver. 3-6. 2.
28.i: On the night before his last battle, Saul went in disguise to a medium at Endor and heard Samuel say that the Lord had left him and that he would die the next day.
28.p: Lord, when You seem silent, keep us from seeking answers in the wrong places. Teach us to wait for You. Amen.
28.l: When you are afraid, pray first, and tell a trusted grown-up. Do not hide your fear.
q: Saul went to the wrong place when God was silent. Where do you go when you are afraid and God seems quiet?

29.o: How Saul, who was forsaken of God, when he was in a strait was more and more perplexed and embarrassed with his own counsels, we read in the foregoing chapter. In this chapter we find how David, who kept close to God, when he was in a strait was extricated and brought off by the providence of God, without any contrivance of his own. We have him, I. Marching with the Philistines, ver. 1, 2. II. Excepted against by the lords of the Philistines, ver. 3-5. III.
29.i: First Samuel 29 shows David, hiding among Israel's enemies, rescued from an impossible choice by the doubts of the Philistine commanders.
29.p: Lord, You guard Your people even when we cannot see how. Thank You for closed doors that keep us from harm. Amen.
29.l: When a plan does not work out today, ask God what good might come from it.
q: Others' suspicion kept David out of a battle he could not have stood in. When has someone's refusal turned out to be a rescue?

30.o: When David was dismissed from the army of the Philistines he did not go over to the camp of Israel, but, being expelled by Saul, observed an exact neutrality, and silently retired to his own city Ziklag, leaving the armies ready to engage. Now here we are told, I. What a melancholy posture he found the city in, all laid waste by the Amalekites, and what distress it occasioned him and his men, ver. 1-6. II. What course he took to recover what he had lost. He enquired of God, and took out a commission from him (ver.
30.i: David returns to burned Ziklag, strengthens himself in the Lord, and rescues his family and everyone taken.
30.p: Lord, when we lose everything, help us to find our strength in You. Amen.
30.l: When you feel like giving up, stop and ask God for strength before you do anything else.
q: Everyone around David wanted to blame someone. What do you do first when things go wrong?

31.o: In the foregoing chapter we had David conquering, yea, more than a conqueror. In this chapter we have Saul conquered and worse than a captive. Providence ordered it that both these things should be doing just at the same time. The very same day; perhaps, that David was triumphing over the Amalekites, were the Philistines triumphing over Saul. One is set over against the other, that men may see what comes of trusting in God and what comes of forsaking him.
31.i: King Saul and his sons died fighting the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, and the men of Jabesh-gilead rescued their bodies and buried them.
31.p: Lord, You judge kings and You remember kindness. Teach us to honor others, even when they have failed. Amen.
31.l: Remember someone who was kind to you in the past. Pray for them today, or send them a note.
q: The men of Jabesh remembered Saul's kindness and acted. What kindness should you act on?
